analysis.one_liner: Creates free emergency insulin cards for uninsured and underinsured people and taxes drugmakers over insulin price spikes.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by one Democrat with one Republican cosponsor, never received a committee vote or any further action and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a federal grant program so states, tribes, and tribal organizations could issue "insulin cards" giving uninsured or underinsured people insulin at no cost — an emergency 7-day supply within five business days, then 90-day refillable cards. It would have paid for the program entirely with annual fees on insulin manufacturers, charged by market share. It also would have imposed an excise tax on insulin makers equal to 50–100% of the extra revenue from price increases above inflation, and cut the legal monopoly period for new biologic drugs from 12 years to 7 to get cheaper copies to market sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured people and people in high-deductible health plans who cannot afford insulin would get a card that covers their insulin at no cost, with payments counted toward their insurance deductible. States and tribal governments would gain funding to run the program. Pharmacists would gain business filling program prescriptions, paid by the states. People with diabetes generally would benefit from the deterrent effect of a tax on price spikes and from faster availability of lower-cost biosimilar insulin after the exclusivity period shrinks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured people with diabetes

how_it_helps.text: States, Indian tribes, and tribal organizations would receive CDC grants to run insulin card programs: a person with a prescription who is uninsured or in a high-deductible plan gets an initial card for an approximately 7-day insulin supply within 5 business days, and a renewable card for an approximately 90-day supply within 12 business days, filled at participating pharmacies at no cost to the person.

Payments made through the program for underinsured people must be counted by their high-deductible health plan toward the deductible and other out-of-pocket costs, so the free insulin does not leave them further from their deductible.

Insulin manufacturers would pay an annual fee, 2020 through 2024, based on each company's share of insulin sales, with the total set to equal the government's cost of running the insulin assistance program — so the companies that sell insulin would fund the safety net rather than taxpayers.

When an insulin product's wholesale price rises faster than inflation, the manufacturer would owe an excise tax of 50% of the extra revenue from the spike (75% for increases of 15–20%, 100% for 20% or more), with an added tax on cumulative multi-year increases, unless HHS grants a for-cause exemption for genuine cost increases.

The bill cuts the marketing exclusivity period for biologic drugs — the years during which cheaper biosimilar copies cannot be approved — from 12 years to 7, which would let lower-priced biosimilar insulin reach the market sooner.
Grantees must help cardholders enroll in other federal or state programs that could cover insulin, moving people onto sustainable coverage rather than leaving them dependent on emergency cards.

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers would bear the cost: annual fees equal to the program's total expenditures for 2020–2024, an excise tax of 50–100% of revenue from above-inflation price increases, civil penalties of 0.5–1% of product revenue per day for failing to submit quarterly pricing reports, and a shorter 7-year exclusivity window on new biologics. States and tribes would have to contribute $1 in non-federal money for every $3 of federal grant funds, and the program prices would be exempted from Medicaid's best-price rules.

drawbacks.text: The program is narrow: it covers only people with no insurance or high-deductible plans, so it does nothing to lower insulin prices for the insured majority, and it never caps list prices — it only taxes spikes after they happen.
States and tribes must put up $1 of their own money for every $3 of federal funds, which could keep the poorest states — often those with the most need — from participating.
The whole scheme is temporary: manufacturer fees run only from 2020 through 2024 and the grant authority sunsets five years after enactment, so the assistance would lapse unless Congress re-ups it.
Prices charged under the program are carved out of Medicaid's best-price and average-manufacturer-price rules, weakening one of the few existing levers that pushes manufacturers to lower list prices.

HHS can exempt insulin products from the spike tax for 'for-cause' reasons, and manufacturers get notice and a hearing before any report goes to the IRS, giving the industry multiple off-ramps from the tax's main penalty.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design directly matches the funding burden to the beneficiary industry — insulin makers would fund the emergency access program out of their own fees and face a real tax on price gouging — which is more honest than taxpayer-funded patches. But as drafted it is a targeted rescue, not a fix: it leaves insulin prices for most insured people untouched, requires state matching money that may exclude the poorest states, hands HHS discretion to exempt manufacturers from the spike tax, carves program prices out of Medicaid best-price rules, and sunsets after five years. It would have been a meaningful lifeline for the people most likely to ration insulin and die from it, with genuine but partial pressure on manufacturers' pricing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Tina Smith introduced the bill on June 27, 2019, joined by Senator Kevin Cramer, the bill's only cosponsor and a Republican.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over tax and health financing policy.
No markup, vote, or any further action ever appears in the bill's history for the rest of the Congress.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired with it; anything not passed is dead and would have to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin and biologic drug manufacturers are better off: they kept the 12-year exclusivity period, never paid the program fees or the price-spike tax, and continued to sell insulin at the high prices the bill targeted. Uninsured and underinsured people with diabetes got no relief.

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Emergency Access to Insulin Act of 2019 in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Kevin Cramer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making its introduction bipartisan.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or vote on it during the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it never left committee, so no floor consideration was ever possible.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor — but no committee or floor vote ever occurred, so the parties' positions were never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have charged insulin makers annual fees equal to the full cost of the assistance program, imposed an excise tax of 50–100% of revenue from above-inflation price spikes, and required quarterly price reporting with per-day penalties. Their gain from keeping prices high is directly the public's cost, since rationing insulin because of price leads to deaths among people with diabetes.

Cutting biologic exclusivity from 12 years to 7 would have shortened the monopoly period in which these companies can charge premium prices before cheaper biosimilars compete. Longer exclusivity protects their revenue; shorter exclusivity lowers drug costs for everyone.
Participating pharmacies would be paid by states for every insulin prescription filled for cardholders, adding reimbursed volume with no cost to the patient.
Plans would have to count the program's payments toward enrollees' deductibles, a new administrative duty, but the program pays for the insulin itself rather than shifting costs to the insurer.
They would gain federal grants and administrative flexibility, including priority for nonprofit contractors, but must contribute $1 of their own money for every $3 in federal funds.
